newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, China agree to formal human rights talks.
newsitem.headline: Australia, China agree to formal human rights talks.

text.p: Australia said on Thursday it had struck a deal with China to set up a formal dialogue on human rights, but would no longer back a U.N. motion censuring Beijing for rights abuses.
Human rights activists quickly questioned Beijing's commitment to improving human rights and criticised Australia for reversing its past policy at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

Downer said the agreement to establish a formal rights dialogue, reached in principle with visiting Chinese Justice Minister Xiao Yang on Wednesday, was the only way Australia could achieve an improvement on human rights.

"What we are talking about here is ... trying to find a way of being effective and the only way that we believe that in our human rights diplomacy with China we can be remotely effective is by establishing some kind of dialogue," he said in a radio interview.
A spokesman for Downer said there was no connection between the decision not to back the U.N. resolution and Wednesday's agreement, which Downer said was a first for China.
"We've obviously given a fair bit of thought to this. But our view about that (U.N.) resolution is that we really don't believe it can achieve anything," Downer said.
The Australia-Tibet Council dismissed the deal as window-dressing by China ahead of the U.N. vote in Geneva.

"It's pretty common before things like this U.N. Human Rights Commission resolution ... for the Chinese to make noises as if they're serious about improving human rights," spokesman Paul Bourke told Reuters.
"We're fairly cynical. We'll be very pleasantly surprised if something comes of it, but we think once ... the U.N. human rights session's finished, it will just fade away."
London-based human rights group Amnesty International -- one of China's most persistent critics -- cautiously welcomed the dialogue but urged a speedy translation into action.
"At this stage, it is mere sentiment and we hope it will be filled out with practical measures," Sydney-based spokeswoman Maya Catsanis told Reuters.
Downer said Xiao wanted an early start to the talks, although Chinese officials in Canberra would not say when they might start or what would be discussed.
The timing and details of the dialogue, suggested by Australian Prime Minister John Howard to Chinese counterpart Li Peng in Beijing last week, will be thrashed out by officials in the coming weeks.
But Australia's top aid agency body warned the talks could be counter-productive if not reinforced by Australian involvement in international moves to pressure China.
"It could, in fact, let China off the hook," a spokesman for the Australian Council for Overseas Aid, an umbrella agency for aid groups, told Reuters.

The draft U.N resolution, which Australia has traditionally co-sponsored, has been proposed by Denmark and has U.S. backing. Other European Union states had supported similar motions -- always defeated by China -- every year since the Tienanmen Square massacre of 1989 but have also backed off this year.
The rights agreement helps cement a turnaround in Beijing's relations with Howard's year-old conservative administration.
Ties had chilled over a series of minor spats on diplomatic and security issues.
